Sen's slope and the total change
Publisher: Trend Detective project

This note was written by the Trend Detective project. It describes how the app estimates a rate of change. It is the project's own description, not a NASA method or a NASA statement.

What Sen's slope is

Sen's slope is the app's estimate of how fast a yearly series changes. For every pair of years in the record, the app takes the difference between the two yearly values and divides it by the difference between the two years. Sen's slope is the median of all these pairwise rates. The app uses the real calendar years, so a missing year is not squeezed out and the remaining years are not treated as consecutive. The app reports the rate per decade: the slope per year multiplied by ten.

What the result fields mean: The rate of change (sen_slope)
Publisher: Trend Detective project

The rate of change, labelled "Rate of change (Sen's slope)", is the field sen_slope. It says how fast the yearly values changed over the years used. For every pair of years the app takes the difference between the two yearly values divided by the difference between the two years, and the rate is the median of these pairwise rates. The app uses the real calendar years, so a missing year is not squeezed out. The rate is shown per decade, in the units of the rate: the slope per year multiplied by ten.

The rate is a description of the record, not by itself evidence of a trend. A rate of zero does not prove that nothing changed. A place has a rate only when it has at least ten complete yearly values.

What the result fields mean: The total change (total_change)
Publisher: Trend Detective project

The field total_change, labelled "Total change over the years used", is the change along the drawn trend line from the first year used to the last. It is the slope per year multiplied by the number of years between the first and the last year used, in the units of the rate. It is not the difference between the first and the last yearly value. The drawn line has the rate's slope and passes through the median year and the median value of the record.

Sen's slope and the total change: A zero rate
Publisher: Trend Detective project

A Sen's slope of zero does not prove that nothing changed. A zero rate also does not override a valid trend test: when the median rate is zero but the trend test finds evidence below its threshold, the verdict stays significant without a rate direction, and the two quantities are explained separately. A rate that is very small but not zero is shown with more digits rather than rounded to zero.

Intervals

The app does not report a confidence interval for the slope. Slope intervals stay empty until a procedure that allows for serial dependence is specified and its coverage is tested.

Publisher: NASA Langley Research Center, POWER Project

The assessment of the accuracy of the hourly MERRA-2 parameters is based upon the surface observations reported in the NCEI Integrated Surface Database (ISD). After applying quality control codes available with the database to the data, only the reports closest to the top of the hour are retained for potential validation. This selection process allows for a greater number of surface sites in Africa, South America, Asia, and Eastern Europe to compare against MERRA-2. What the result fields mean: The verdict (verdict.kind and verdict.sentence)
Publisher: Trend Detective project

The field verdict.kind, labelled "Verdict", is one of five kinds. Significant: the evidence for a monotonic trend meets the test's threshold. Not significant: these data do not provide sufficient evidence for a monotonic trend, which does not establish that no change occurred. Too few years: fewer than ten complete yearly values. No data: no usable yearly values for this place and period. Inference unavailable: the trend test does not apply to this case, so significance has not been assessed, and the rate is descriptive where there is one.

The field verdict.sentence, labelled "Verdict sentence", is the app's fixed sentence for that verdict, in words chosen by the app, not by an AI. For a verdict from the trend test it states the estimated change per decade over the years used and what the evidence does or does not show; for a verdict without the test it gives the reason and says that significance has not been assessed.

The Mann-Kendall trend test in Trend Detective: What the Mann-Kendall test asks
Publisher: Trend Detective project

The Mann-Kendall (MK) test asks whether a yearly series tends to rise or to fall over time, without assuming the change is a straight line. It compares every pair of years: a later value higher than an earlier one counts plus one, a lower one minus one, and a tie zero. The sum of these signs is the MK score. A score far from zero, in either direction, is evidence for a monotonic trend. The app uses the two-sided test, so a rise and a fall are treated alike.

What each verdict means
Publisher: Trend Detective project

This note was written by the Trend Detective project. It explains the verdicts the app gives. The verdicts and their wording are the project's own, not NASA's.

The five verdict kinds

- no_data: there are no usable complete annual values for this place and period.
- too_few_years: fewer than ten complete annual values, so the app gives no rate. The verdict states the count and the policy threshold.
- inference_unavailable: a significance test is not justified or not available for this case. The app gives a descriptive rate where it can, and the reason the test was not run. Significance has not been assessed.
- significant: the validated test gives a p-value below 0.05. The evidence for a monotonic trend meets the stated 5% threshold.
- not_significant: the validated test gives a p-value of 0.05 or more. These data do not provide sufficient evidence for a monotonic trend under the method.

Reading a result: what significance does and does not say: Significant is not cause or importance
Publisher: Trend Detective project

A significant verdict means the evidence for a monotonic trend meets the stated threshold under the method's assumptions. Significance is not practical importance: a statistically significant change can be small. Significance is not cause: the test says nothing about why the series changed, and it does not attribute a change to any process or activity. A significant result also does not certify that the method's assumptions hold for the real series.

What the result fields mean: The p-value of the trend test (mk_p)
Publisher: Trend Detective project

The field mk_p, labelled "Mann-Kendall p-value", is the p-value of the trend test. It is the probability of a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed if the record had no monotonic trend, under the test's assumptions. It is not the probability that a trend is real, and it does not measure how large or important a change is, or what caused it.

The app runs the test only for complete annual two-metre air temperature records of twenty to forty-five contiguous years with no change of source. For every other variable, season or record the p-value is empty and shown as "Not assessed"; it is never set to one. A p-value below the five percent threshold gives the verdict significant; a p-value at or above it gives not significant.

Reading a result: what significance does and does not say
Publisher: Trend Detective project

This note was written by the Trend Detective project. It explains how to read the app's results. It is the project's own guidance, not a NASA statement.

Not significant is not proof of no change

A not significant verdict means the data do not provide sufficient evidence for a monotonic trend under the method. It does not establish that no change occurred. The test asks only about a monotonic trend, and its conservative design reduces its power, particularly for short records, so a real change can go undetected. A zero estimated rate does not prove no change either.

Reading a result: what significance does and does not say: P-values and intervals
Publisher: Trend Detective project

A p-value is the probability of a statistic at least as extreme as the one observed under the null model and its assumptions. It is not the probability that a claim is true. A 95% interval describes how often the procedure would cover the true value over repeated use; it does not assign a probability to a fixed true value. P-values alone do not describe every form of uncertainty.

Serial dependence and the retired lag-one correction
Publisher: Trend Detective project

This note was written by the Trend Detective project. It explains how the project's method treats year-to-year dependence. It is the project's own description, not a NASA method.

Why dependence matters

Neighbouring years of a record can be correlated with each other (lag-one autocorrelation). A trend test whose null distribution assumes independent years can then report evidence of a trend more often than its threshold suggests, which is why the project checked its procedure against correlated noise. Averaging months into years does not establish that the years are independent.

Serial dependence and the retired lag-one correction: What the app does instead
Publisher: Trend Detective project

The current procedure, mk_mc_envelope_v1, allows for dependence by simulation. Its null distributions were built from lag-one autoregressive series with correlation 0, 0.2 or 0.5, with Gaussian or skewed shocks, and the app takes the largest tail probability across these scenarios. This protects against false positives for the declared kinds of dependence. It does not establish validity for every form of dependence: all climate noise, intermediate correlation values, structural breaks and arbitrary dependence are outside what was checked. The price of this protection is lower power, so short records or weak trends can fail to reach the threshold even when change occurred.

Serial dependence and the retired lag-one correction: The retired correction
Publisher: Trend Detective project

An earlier draft of the project corrected for dependence with a multiplier based on the lag-one autocorrelation of the residuals, (1 + r1) / (1 - r1), applied to the Mann-Kendall test, the least squares slope and the interval. That multiplier has been retired as a universal correction. The earlier draft's reported false-positive rates and corrected fixture results had no reproducible evidence and are not accepted as validation. The retired multiplier must not be used to claim interval coverage.

Before release the procedure was checked in predeclared simulation studies at a nominal 5% threshold, with an engineering guardrail on the false-positive rate in every declared setting; every declared setting met it. POWER Solar Flux Data Sources: SYN1deg
Publisher: NASA Langley Research Center, POWER Project

The CERES projects are based upon the algorithms developed for analysis and data collected by the Clouds and the Earth's Radiant Energy System (CERES) project. CERES is currently producing world-class climate data products derived from measurements taken aboard NASA's Terra and Aqua satellites. SYN1deg also incorporates geostationary cloud properties into the model calculations to produce global hourly fluxes. Details of SYN1deg inputs and algorithm can be found in Rutan et al., (2015). While of exceptional fidelity, CERES data products require extensive calibration checks and validation to assure quality and verify accuracy and precision. The result is that CERES data are typically released more than six months after acquisition of the initial measurements. For climate studies, such delays are of little consequence especially considering the improved quality of the released data products. The geostationary inputs are normalized to CERES and temporally interpolated to fill the gaps between Terra/Aqua overpasses, yielding continuous hourly surface fluxes (Doelling et al., 2013).

POWER Data Processing: Processing Hierarchy
Publisher: NASA Langley Research Center, POWER Project

POWER uses a set Processing Hierarchy for stored data values. The arrow going left to right shows the higher level of aggregation and how the data is computed. Each step in the hierarchy applies a single, well-defined operation (mean, maximum, or minimum) to the level immediately below it, so the stored values at every temporal resolution remain traceable back to the original hourly fields; the daily aggregation is performed in local solar time so that the 24-hour window aligns with the solar day rather than UTC, a convention rooted in standard timekeeping and climatological reporting practice

Hourly | Daily | Monthly | Annual | Climatology

Type | Value | Extreme and Average | Average | Average | Average

Operation | 24 Hours | Mean, Max, or Min of 24 Hours | Mean of the Days | Mean of the Months | Mean of the Annual

POWER Data Processing: Data Processing
Publisher: NASA Langley Research Center, POWER Project

The POWER Project uses a nested temporal processing hierarchy: each coarser temporal level is computed directly from the level below it. Hourly data are the foundation. Daily values are derived from the 24 hourly values (after any local-time conversion). Monthly values are derived from daily values, annual from monthly, and climatology from annual. No temporal level is produced from an independent model run.This cascading scheme ensures internal consistency, because each coarser product is a deterministic average of the immediately finer product rather than an independent re-computation from source reanalysis.

The one exception is extreme-value parameters such as Maximum Temperature at Two Meters (T2M_MAX), which retain the instantaneous hourly extreme rather than averaging. Related parameters such as T2M_MAX_AVG are the average of the daily extreme values.

Grid cells, reanalysis and data sources: Reanalysis and model output
Publisher: Trend Detective project

Two-metre air temperature (T2M) in POWER comes from MERRA-2 reanalysis. POWER supplies reanalysis values, which describe a grid cell; they are not exact local station measurements. Snow, sea ice, surface pressure, water vapour and the strongest wind in the app also come from MERRA-2. Haze is aerosol optical depth from CERES SYN1deg, available from 2001.

Grid cells, reanalysis and data sources
Publisher: Trend Detective project

This note was written by the Trend Detective project. It explains what the app's numbers describe. It is the project's own summary; for the data themselves, see the NASA POWER and GMAO documentation.

A grid cell, not a point

The app reads NASA POWER monthly values for the grid cell that contains the chosen place. A result describes that grid cell, not the exact point or a city weather station. Two places in the same grid cell get the same values, so the difference between them is zero in every year. The place's name is only a label; it does not change the data.

Grid cells, reanalysis and data sources: Yearly values
Publisher: Trend Detective project

The app makes each yearly value from the twelve monthly values, weighting each month by its number of days and respecting leap years. A year with a missing month has no yearly value; a missing value is never replaced by zero. This day-weighted mean is the app's own named statistic. POWER describes its own annual values as a mean of the months, so the two need not be identical.

Grid cells, reanalysis and data sources: Changes of data source
Publisher: Trend Detective project

Some records change their source part way through. POWER's solar and cloud records come from one source up to 2000 and another from 2001, and NASA warns about source changes in radiation trend analysis. The app keeps solar and cloud records that cross the 2001 transition descriptive and shows a caution when the analysis years cross a source change.

POWER Meteorological Data Sources: MERRA-2
Publisher: NASA Langley Research Center, POWER Project

The POWER meteorological parameters provided by the project and listed within this validation section are based on NASA Goddard's Global Modeling and Assimilation Office (GMAO) assimilation model and the Modern Era Retrospective-Analysis for Research and Applications (MERRA-2) (see these for more details on the reanalysis: Gelaro, 2017, Rienecker et al., 2008, Molod et al., 2015, and the MERRA-2 AMS Collection). MERRA-2 spans 1980 to the present and is documented in the peer-reviewed system overview and the GEOS-5 model description, which together establish the reanalysis configuration POWER relies upon. Each of the parameters is either obtained directly from or calculated using meteorological parameters taken from NASA's MERRA-2 assimilation model.

The model seeks to assimilate and optimize observational data and model estimates of atmospheric variables.

POWER Meteorological Data Sources: Validation Overview
Publisher: NASA Langley Research Center, POWER Project

The assessment of the accuracy of the MERRA-2 parameters is based upon comparisons with observations from the corresponding parameters reported to the National Center for Environmental Information (NCEI). Hourly assessments are compared against the Integrated Surface Database (ISD), while daily average assessments are compared against the Global Summary of the Day (GSOD). The ISD is NOAA/NCEI's quality-controlled archive of global hourly and synoptic surface observations, and GSOD is derived from ISD as daily summaries, making both authoritative ground-truth references for reanalysis evaluation.

In the following sections, scatter plots associated with each meteorological parameter provide a visual indication of the agreement between the MERRA-2 values and surface observations. The statistical parameters enumerated on each scatter plot and summarized in tables gives a more quantitative assessment of this agreement.

POWER Meteorological Data Sources: Meteorological
Publisher: NASA Langley Research Center, POWER Project

Meteorological parameters are derived from NASA's GMAO MERRA-2 assimilation model and GEOS-IT. MERRA-2 is a version of NASA's Goddard Earth Observing System (GEOS) Data Assimilation System (Gelaro, 2017) MERRA-2 is the first long-term global reanalysis to assimilate space-based aerosol observations and uses the GEOS-5 atmospheric model and Gridpoint Statistical Interpolation analysis. Molod, 2015. GMAO GEOS-IT has the same grid resolution as MERRA-2 (and the same model physics less selected observations and surface rain gauge normalized precipitation). GEOS-IT is GMAO's near-real-time instrument-team product that shares the GEOS modeling and assimilation framework, enabling low-latency continuation of the MERRA-2 record. The POWER team processes GEOS-IT data on a daily basis, and it is appended to the end of the MERRA-2 daily time series to provide low latency products, which are generally ready within about two days of real-time. The MERRA-2 values in the resulting daily time series are typically updated every several months.

POWER Meteorological Data Sources: Surface Pressure
Publisher: NASA Langley Research Center, POWER Project

This section compares MERRA-2 surface pressure to observations reported to the NCEI with an adjustment made to the difference in elevation between MERRA-2 and the site elevation. Because the MERRA-2 grid-box elevation generally differs from a station's true elevation, a hypsometric (barometric) reduction is required for a like-for-like comparison; this relation follows directly from hydrostatic balance and the ideal gas law.

Hypsometric Equation for Adjustment of Surface Pressure

The elevation of the MERRA-2 grid box is the mean elevation of the earth’s surface under the grid. In complex terrain one might expect to see a difference between the MERRA-2 elevation and that of the surface site resulting in a difference between the MERRA-2 pressure and that reported by the surface site. The Surface Pressure (Hypsometric Equation) scatter plot illustrates the improvements in the agreement between the MERRA-2 estimates of pressure and observational data by adjusting the MERRA-2 pressure using the hypsometric equation.

Serial dependence and the retired lag-one correction
Publisher: Trend Detective project

This note was written by the Trend Detective project. It explains how the project's method treats year-to-year dependence. It is the project's own description, not a NASA method.

Why dependence matters

Neighbouring years of a record can be correlated with each other (lag-one autocorrelation). A trend test whose null distribution assumes independent years can then report evidence of a trend more often than its threshold suggests, which is why the project checked its procedure against correlated noise. Averaging months into years does not establish that the years are independent.

What the result fields mean: The rate of change (sen_slope)
Publisher: Trend Detective project

The rate of change, labelled "Rate of change (Sen's slope)", is the field sen_slope. It says how fast the yearly values changed over the years used. For every pair of years the app takes the difference between the two yearly values divided by the difference between the two years, and the rate is the median of these pairwise rates. The app uses the real calendar years, so a missing year is not squeezed out. The rate is shown per decade, in the units of the rate: the slope per year multiplied by ten.

The rate is a description of the record, not by itself evidence of a trend. A rate of zero does not prove that nothing changed. A place has a rate only when it has at least ten complete yearly values.

The Mann-Kendall trend test in Trend Detective: What the Mann-Kendall test asks
Publisher: Trend Detective project

The Mann-Kendall (MK) test asks whether a yearly series tends to rise or to fall over time, without assuming the change is a straight line. It compares every pair of years: a later value higher than an earlier one counts plus one, a lower one minus one, and a tie zero. The sum of these signs is the MK score. A score far from zero, in either direction, is evidence for a monotonic trend. The app uses the two-sided test, so a rise and a fall are treated alike.

A significant verdict means the evidence for a monotonic trend meets the stated threshold under the method's assumptions. Publisher: NASA Langley Research Center, POWER Project

The assessment of the accuracy of the MERRA-2 parameters is based upon comparisons with observations from the corresponding parameters reported to the National Center for Environmental Information (NCEI). Hourly assessments are compared against the Integrated Surface Database (ISD), while daily average assessments are compared against the Global Summary of the Day (GSOD). MERRA-2 System Characteristics: System Characteristics
Publisher: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Global Modeling and Assimilation Office (GMAO)

System

- System name (version): Modern Era Retrospective-analysis for Research and Applications version 2 (MERRA-2) (using Goddard Earth Observing System version 5.12.4)

- Date of implementation: Oct 12, 2015

- Project overview paper: Gelaro et al. (2017)

Configuration

- Earth system components included in the analysis system (e.g., ocean, sea-ice, land, etc.): Catchment Land Surface Model with Observation Corrected Precipitation. Assimilated and Interactive Aerosols

- Horizontal resolution of the model, with indication of grid spacing in km (for the different Earth system component included in the model): The model is run on a cubed sphere grid.

POWER Meteorological Data Sources: Meteorological
Publisher: NASA Langley Research Center, POWER Project

Meteorological parameters are derived from NASA's GMAO MERRA-2 assimilation model and GEOS-IT. MERRA-2 is a version of NASA's Goddard Earth Observing System (GEOS) Data Assimilation System (Gelaro, 2017) MERRA-2 is the first long-term global reanalysis to assimilate space-based aerosol observations and uses the GEOS-5 atmospheric model and Gridpoint Statistical Interpolation analysis. Molod, 2015. GMAO GEOS-IT has the same grid resolution as MERRA-2 (and the same model physics less selected observations and surface rain gauge normalized precipitation). GEOS-IT is GMAO's near-real-time instrument-team product that shares the GEOS modeling and assimilation framework, enabling low-latency continuation of the MERRA-2 record. The POWER team processes GEOS-IT data on a daily basis, and it is appended to the end of the MERRA-2 daily time series to provide low latency products, which are generally ready within about two days of real-time. The MERRA-2 values in the resulting daily time series are typically updated every several months.

POWER Solar Flux Data Sources: SRB 4-IP (part 2)
Publisher: NASA Langley Research Center, POWER Project

The shortwave (SW) algorithm uses a modified method of Pinker and Laszlo (1992) to solve the radiative transfer equation and provide the SRB Release 4-IP estimates of surface SW solar insolation. This method involves the use of a radiative transfer model, along with cloud parameters derived from the International Satellite Cloud Climatology Project (ISCCP) HX data (Young et al., 2018) and temperature and moisture profiles taken from ISCCP nnHIRS with supplements from 4-D data assimilation products provided by NASA Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) and produced with Modern Era Retrospective-Analysis for Research and Applications (MERRA-2) and ozone column amounts from satellite measurements. Three satellite visible radiances are used: the instantaneous clear-sky radiance, the instantaneous cloudy-sky radiance, and the clear-sky composite radiance, which is a representation of a recent dark background value.

POWER Hydrology Data Sources: SMAP Processing
Publisher: NASA Langley Research Center, POWER Project

- Source product: NASA produces the L4_SM global daily analysis on a 9 km Equal-Area Scalable Earth (EASE) grid.

- Regridding: The POWER pipeline uses the standard latitude–longitude grid at approximately 0.09° spacing. Reichle et al., 2017 SMAP L4_SM, 2026

- Temporal aggregation: POWER serves SMAP at the daily UTC temporal level. Monthly and annual aggregates are computed by averaging daily values.

- Storage: Processed fields are stored as Zarr arrays in the POWER datastore on AWS (s3://nasa-power-smap/smap/).

POWER Cloud and Aerosol Data Sources: SYN1deg
Publisher: NASA Langley Research Center, POWER Project

Cloud Amount and Cloud Optical Visible Depth are derived from NASA's CERES SYN1deg and are available to users at the Hourly, Daily, Monthly, Annual, and Climatology temporal levels.The CERES SYN1deg synoptic product combines CERES broadband measurements with cloud properties retrieved from MODIS and from geostationary imagers, the latter supplying the diurnal sampling that polar-orbiting satellites alone cannot provide, to produce temporally complete, globally gridded cloud and flux fields Rutan et al., 2015; CERES, 2024. As with the solar data, the cloud cover information is available in its original source spatial resolution. Cloud Optical Visible Depth is the vertical optical thickness between the top and bottom of a cloud as computed in the CERES algorithm. Cloud optical depth in CERES is retrieved from imager radiances using the CERES cloud-property algorithm, which derives optical thickness alongside cloud phase and effective particle size Minnis et al., 2011; Minnis et al., 2021.

The percentage of cloud cover is computed in the CERES algorithm.

POWER Meteorological Data Sources: Validation IMERG vs. MERRA-2
Publisher: NASA Langley Research Center, POWER Project

The POWER project compared accumulated precipitation from the NCEI GSOD observations to two precipitation sources: the Integrated Multi-satellitE Retrievals for GPM (IMERG) and MERRA-2. This comparison was done to evaluate the performance between the higher resolution IMERG against the MERRA-2 data product. Independent evaluations have found that satellite-gauge products such as IMERG can better capture spatial precipitation structure than coarser reanalyses, though relative skill varies by region, season, and accumulation period.

Two test cases were completed to conduct this comparison:

- All Events: pairs compared at the weekly and monthly level.

- Precipitation Only: pairs compared at the weekly and monthly level where precipitation was greater than zero.

The IMERG data is only available at the daily temporal in UTC time for POWER's services.

Grid cells, reanalysis and data sources: Yearly values
Publisher: Trend Detective project

The app makes each yearly value from the twelve monthly values, weighting each month by its number of days and respecting leap years. A year with a missing month has no yearly value; a missing value is never replaced by zero. This day-weighted mean is the app's own named statistic. POWER describes its own annual values as a mean of the months, so the two need not be identical.

POWER Validation Data Sources: Temporal Aggregation
Publisher: NASA Langley Research Center, POWER Project

Hourly and daily AERONET in POWER are sourced differently, where daily averages are already available from the AERONET project, hourly must be aggregated from raw minute-based data. Daily AOD 550 and 840 are interpolated as described above and do not need temporal aggregation.

Raw AERONET data is aggregated to hourly values for POWER users in a similar method as how BSRN is handled. The minute-based data is averaged to 15-minute and require at least 1 valid value. The hourly values are averaged from 4 valid 15-minute values or else no value can be assigned. Daily values are a result of the average of at least 5 hourly values. Since POWER does not have sub-hourly core data, the minute-based and 15-minute averages are discarded and only the hourly values are kept.

Once it is curated and saved in POWER's storage solution, the data is ready for users to validate with it in the DAV or API.

Data Latency

While AERONET updates their data sets daily, POWER accesses and processes the complete data set on a monthly basis.

What the result fields mean: The verdict (verdict.kind and verdict.sentence)
Publisher: Trend Detective project

The field verdict.kind, labelled "Verdict", is one of five kinds. Significant: the evidence for a monotonic trend meets the test's threshold. Not significant: these data do not provide sufficient evidence for a monotonic trend, which does not establish that no change occurred. Too few years: fewer than ten complete yearly values. No data: no usable yearly values for this place and period. Inference unavailable: the trend test does not apply to this case, so significance has not been assessed, and the rate is descriptive where there is one.

The field verdict.sentence, labelled "Verdict sentence", is the app's fixed sentence for that verdict, in words chosen by the app, not by an AI. For a verdict from the trend test it states the estimated change per decade over the years used and what the evidence does or does not show; for a verdict without the test it gives the reason and says that significance has not been assessed.

What the result fields mean: The p-value of the trend test (mk_p)
Publisher: Trend Detective project

The field mk_p, labelled "Mann-Kendall p-value", is the p-value of the trend test. It is the probability of a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed if the record had no monotonic trend, under the test's assumptions. It is not the probability that a trend is real, and it does not measure how large or important a change is, or what caused it.

The app runs the test only for complete annual two-metre air temperature records of twenty to forty-five contiguous years with no change of source. For every other variable, season or record the p-value is empty and shown as "Not assessed"; it is never set to one. A p-value below the five percent threshold gives the verdict significant; a p-value at or above it gives not significant.

What each verdict means
Publisher: Trend Detective project

This note was written by the Trend Detective project. It explains the verdicts the app gives. The verdicts and their wording are the project's own, not NASA's.

The five verdict kinds

- no_data: there are no usable complete annual values for this place and period.
- too_few_years: fewer than ten complete annual values, so the app gives no rate. The verdict states the count and the policy threshold.
- inference_unavailable: a significance test is not justified or not available for this case. The app gives a descriptive rate where it can, and the reason the test was not run. Significance has not been assessed.
- significant: the validated test gives a p-value below 0.05. The evidence for a monotonic trend meets the stated 5% threshold.
- not_significant: the validated test gives a p-value of 0.05 or more. These data do not provide sufficient evidence for a monotonic trend under the method.

What each verdict means: When significance is not assessed
Publisher: Trend Detective project

Many results are descriptive only. Significance is not assessed for any variable other than annual two-metre air temperature, for seasons, maps and area averages, for records of ten to nineteen years, for records with missing years or discontinuities, for periods that cross a change of data source, and when the calibration is missing. In these cases the verdict is inference_unavailable, the p-value is empty and the app says why. A descriptive rate is a summary of the data, not a test.

POWER Meteorological Data Sources: Contingency Table (part 2)
Publisher: NASA Langley Research Center, POWER Project

Hits: Row 2 and Column 2 depict the "Precipitation" categories for the MERRA-2 and NCEI ground site data, respectively. Their intersection shows the total number of data days (2,872,392) where both data sets measured precipitation greater than 0.508 mm on the same days ("hits"). This represented 21% of the total data days counted. The "hits" category is broken down further in sub-categories, depicted in the lower table in the Hits Contingency Table, along with statistics. The sub-categories consist of data days when the MERRA-2 precipitation is less than the NCEI ground site, when the MERRA-2 precipitation is greater than the NCEI ground site, and when the MERRA-2 precipitation is "equal" to the NCEI ground site. "Equal" meaning within the measurement accuracy of the NCEI ground site instruments (0.508 mm). Out of the total number of data day "hits", 15% data days occur when the MERRA-2 precipitation is equal to the NCEI ground site precipitation.

POWER Meteorological Data Sources: Daily Average Overview
Publisher: NASA Langley Research Center, POWER Project

Comparison statistics for the daily assessment are based upon comparisons of the given parameter for 1981–2020. The same set of sites from the hourly assessment are used here.

Daily Average Surface Validation Summary

Presented here are the results of comparing MERRA-2 daily meteorological parameters to corresponding surface observation reported in the National Center for Environmental Information (NCEI) (formerly National Climatic Data Center) Global Summary of the Day (GSOD) files. The Slope, Intercept, and R-squared (Rsqrd) listed in this table are associated with a linear least squares fit of daily observations at each surface station to the corresponding MERRA-2 values for the overlapping grid cell. The Mean Bias Error (MBE) and Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) represent mean values over the comparison years.

POWER Meteorological Data Sources: Validation IMERG vs. MERRA-2
Publisher: NASA Langley Research Center, POWER Project

The POWER project compared accumulated precipitation from the NCEI GSOD observations to two precipitation sources: the Integrated Multi-satellitE Retrievals for GPM (IMERG) and MERRA-2. This comparison was done to evaluate the performance between the higher resolution IMERG against the MERRA-2 data product. Independent evaluations have found that satellite-gauge products such as IMERG can better capture spatial precipitation structure than coarser reanalyses, though relative skill varies by region, season, and accumulation period.

Two test cases were completed to conduct this comparison:

- All Events: pairs compared at the weekly and monthly level.

- Precipitation Only: pairs compared at the weekly and monthly level where precipitation was greater than zero.

The IMERG data is only available at the daily temporal in UTC time for POWER's services.

POWER Hydrology Data Sources: IMERG
Publisher: NASA Langley Research Center, POWER Project

IMERG merges precipitation estimates from the GPM constellation of passive-microwave and infrared sensors into a 0.1° × 0.1° (~10 km) half-hourly gridded product, providing the high-resolution precipitation that forces hydrologic models. More information on IMERG is available on the Meteorological page.
